statements.text: Psoriasis worsened over last 4 months, spread to elbows, knees, lower back, and scalp with itching.

evidence.quote: Over the last 4 months it's spread. My elbows and knees are bad again, there's a big patch on my lower back, and my scalp itches like crazy.

statements.text: Psoriasis history of 8 years, currently worst it has been.

evidence.quote: I've had this for 8 years and this is the worst it's been.

statements.text: Using clobetasol ointment twice daily on worst spots with temporary relief.

evidence.quote: Yes, twice a day on the worst spots. It helps for a few days and then it all comes back.

statements.text: Stopped methotrexate on own in June; was taking 15 milligrams weekly (six 2.5 mg pills).

evidence.quote: I stopped that on my own in June. I was on 10 milligrams a week. No, wait, it was 15, 6 of the little 2.5 pills.

statements.text: Methotrexate caused nausea and hair thinning.

evidence.quote: It made me so nauseous and my hair got thin.

statements.text: No joint pain, swelling, stiffness, sausage-like swelling, or heel pain.

evidence.quote: No.
No, none of that.

statements.text: Mother has rheumatoid arthritis in hands.

evidence.quote: My mom had rheumatoid arthritis in her hands, so I'd notice, believe me.

statements.text: Taking amlodipine 5 milligrams every morning for blood pressure.

evidence.quote: Amlodipine, 5 milligrams every morning for blood pressure. That's it.

statements.text: Allergic to sulfa; causes rash all over.

evidence.quote: Yes, I get a rash all over.

statements.text: Quit smoking 3 years ago.

evidence.quote: 3 years quit now.

statements.text: Well-defined red plaques with thick silvery scale on both elbows, right 8 by 6 cm; similar plaques on both knees.

evidence.quote: On both elbows there are well-defined red plaques with thick silvery scale, the right one is about 8 by 6 centimeters. Similar plaques on both knees.

statements.text: 10 by 7 cm plaque on lower back.

evidence.quote: On the lower back there's a 10 by 7 centimeter plaque.

statements.text: Red scaly plaques on scalp behind both ears and along hairline.

evidence.quote: On the scalp, red scaly plaques behind both ears and along the hairline.

statements.text: Pitting on 3 fingernails.

evidence.quote: I see pitting on 3 of your fingernails.

statements.text: No swollen or tender finger joints; no swollen fingers or toes.

evidence.quote: Your finger joints aren't swollen or tender, and no swollen fingers or toes.

statements.text: Estimated body surface area involvement: 12 percent.

evidence.quote: Overall about 12 percent of your body surface.

statements.text: Moderate to severe plaque psoriasis not controlled with topical steroids; methotrexate not tolerated.

evidence.quote: So this is moderate to severe plaque psoriasis that isn't controlled with creams, and methotrexate didn't work out for you.

statements.text: Initiate risankizumab 150 mg subcutaneous injection at week 0, week 4, then every 12 weeks.

evidence.quote: The one I'd recommend is risankizumab. It's an injection under the skin, 150 milligrams, given at week 0, week 4, and then just every 12 weeks.

statements.text: Order TB blood test, hepatitis B and C tests, complete blood count, and metabolic panel prior to starting risankizumab.

evidence.quote: Before we start, I need a TB blood test, hepatitis B and C tests, a blood count and a metabolic panel.

statements.text: Advise avoidance of live vaccines while on risankizumab; recommend seasonal flu shot.

evidence.quote: You should also avoid live vaccines once you're on it, so getting your flu shot this fall is a good idea.

statements.text: Continue clobetasol ointment twice daily on body plaques for 2 weeks on, 1 week off to prevent skin thinning.

evidence.quote: In the meantime, keep the clobetasol ointment twice a day on the body plaques, but only 2 weeks at a time, then a week off, so the skin doesn't thin.

statements.text: Add clobetasol 0.05% solution for scalp, once daily at night.

evidence.quote: For your scalp, I'm adding clobetasol 0.05 percent solution, once a day at night.

statements.text: Send prior authorization request to insurance; patient provided member ID K as in kilo 7 0 3 9 2 1 5.

evidence.quote: We'll also need a prior authorization from your insurance. Do you have your card?
Yeah, member ID is K as in kilo 7 0 3 9 2 1 5.

statements.text: Schedule follow-up in 6 weeks after labs and insurance approval for first injection and training.

evidence.quote: Once the labs and insurance approval come back, we'll have you in for the first injection and teach you how to do it. Otherwise follow-up in 6 weeks.

statements.text: Instruct patient to report joint pain, swelling, or morning stiffness promptly due to risk of psoriatic arthritis.

evidence.quote: And if you ever do get joint pain, swelling, or morning stiffness, tell me right away, because psoriasis can affect the joints and that changes treatment.

note.after_visit_summary: You have moderate to severe psoriasis that has worsened over the past few months, affecting your elbows, knees, lower back, and scalp. Creams and methotrexate have not controlled it well. We are starting a new medication called risankizumab, which is an injection given every 12 weeks after two starter doses. Before starting, you need blood tests for TB, hepatitis, blood count, and metabolic panel. Please get these done at the lab at 2250 Riverside Drive. We will send the orders and work with your insurance (member ID K as in kilo 7 0 3 9 2 1 5) for approval. In the meantime, continue using clobetasol ointment on your body plaques twice daily, but use it for only 2 weeks at a time followed by 1 week off to prevent skin thinning. For your scalp, use clobetasol 0.05% solution once daily at night. Avoid live vaccines while on risankizumab, but get your flu shot this fall. Watch for joint pain, swelling, or stiffness and call us right away if these occur. Follow up in 6 weeks for the first injection and training, once labs and insurance are approved. Keep using your current blood pressure medication, amlodipine 5 mg daily. Call us at 555-0134 with any questions.

icd10.rationale: Psoriasis vulgaris is the most specific billable code supported by documentation of well-defined red plaques with thick silvery scale on elbows, knees, lower back, and scalp, consistent with plaque psoriasis.
